Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman balances ongoing AI infrastructure growth against heavier capital needs, weak model moats, usage-based pricing and construction constraints. He argues suppliers may retain better economics than model providers while acknowledging their dependence on continued spending. The Anthropic suspension and Alphabet equity package are real, but the suspension was temporary and the financing headline includes future capacity. Other themes include rate-sensitive homebuilders, private-credit liquidity, payment competition and the limits of geographic diversification.

Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

## Framework and tools

- Distinguish technological transformation from investment returns.
- Compare suppliers' economics with capital-intensive customers.
- Track pricing and usage after subsidies decline.
- Treat higher rates as a key housing and valuation transmission channel.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- NVIDIA revenue growth and hyperscaler capex.
- Alphabet equity financing and cash flow.
- Meritage tangible book and acquisition multiples.
- Fund redemption requests and caps.
- Regional index sector weights and company market caps.

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman delivers a solo monologue; inserted advertisements and opening montage are excluded.
- Opening montage duplicates later claims and is excluded.
- The transcript says airlines are not notoriously bad businesses, but surrounding sentences clearly describe weak airline economics; retain this as a caption/negation caution.
- Amazon motive is explicitly speculative.
- Announced equity capacity is distinguished from completed funding.
